extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded biomedical researchers, PIs and grant applicants (academic scientists interested in grant review, research design, and career issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative principles for crafting NIH-style proposals and designing rigorously reviewed biomedical experiments, plus related career/funding practices (preprints, startup funds, collaborations, citation metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific premise (rigor of prior research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific premise refers to the rigor of the prior research being cited as key support for the research question(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH will ask applicants to describe strengths and weaknesses in the rigor of the prior research (both published and unpublished) that serves as key support. Be specific: call out inadequate sample sizes, poor design, bad interpretation, wrong parameters or reagents, or context-specific issues (e.g., behavioral studies run in the inactive part of the rodent daily cycle). Reviewers will expect pointed critique of cited literature and applicants should plan to justify and contextualize prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance: describe strengths and weaknesses of cited prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Significance criterion applicants must describe the strengths and weaknesses in the rigor of the prior research that serves as key support for the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use bland statements such as 'more research is needed.' Explicitly identify methodological or inferential weaknesses in prior studies that motivate your project (e.g., small n, flawed controls). Provide examples and quantification where possible to help reviewers assess premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach: plans to address weaknesses in prior research
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Approach, applicants are expected to describe plans to address weaknesses in the prior research that serves as key support for the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out concrete experimental or analytical strategies that remediate the identified weaknesses (e.g., increased sample size, alternative assays, different controls, replication plans). Explain how your methodology directly addresses the limitations you identify in the prior literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate definition of sample size and accounting for independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample size ('n') must be correctly defined and analyses should account for nonindependence when multiple measurements (e.g., neurons) come from the same animal or subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat each recorded neuron as an independent 'n' when multiple neurons come from a small number of animals. Design and statistical plans must account for variability across subjects (animals) and avoid pseudoreplication. State how you will model subject-level variability and justify your chosen unit of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circadian / light-cycle considerations for behavioral experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day and animal light cycle materially affect behavioral and pharmacological outcomes; rodents are nocturnal and are most active in the dark (their 'active cycle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By default, run behavioral experiments in the animals' active cycle unless there is a compelling reason not to. Consider and report time-of-day effects and potential interactions with other variables. Be prepared to justify the chosen schedule and cite evidence (examples: Scheving et al. 1968; Roberts et al. 2002) that time-of-day can change results dramatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation distributions and medians rather than JIF for impact assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is skewed by rare highly-cited articles; the distribution of citations per item and the median provide a better sense of typical article performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a paper's impact relative to a journal, compare its citation count to the journal's citation distribution or median rather than the JIF. Editors evaluate JIF but the median better represents 'typical' performance. If critiquing editorial decisions, check actual citations of rejected manuscripts (once published elsewhere) against the journal median.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint-to-publication ratio as a productivity/quality heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor how many preprints eventually advance to peer-reviewed publication; a high number of preprints that never get published may indicate problems completing or publishing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an applicant's output, consider the proportion of preprints that move on to peer-reviewed journals. For authors: consider spacing preprint uploads or focusing on converting preprints to publications to avoid creating the appearance of poor 'closure' on projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startup fund policy: expiration and conversion into preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Startup packages may have an expiration clause (e.g., funds reclaimed upon obtaining an R01) or time limits; institutions may expect startup to be used for 'starting' only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the written terms of a startup package. If funds expire on grant award or after a set period, prioritize producing useful preliminary data early. Treat startup as seed money to generate the data needed to secure extramural grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear collaborator roles to avoid 'trophy collaborator' outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some collaborators are invited to make a proposal more attractive but may be removed from the project after funding ('trophy collaborator').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear, preferably written, roles and expectations for collaborators in proposals (contributions, authorship, governance, conditions for removal). Consider formal agreements or MOUs to reduce the risk of being cut from a funded project without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit data sharing expectations vary across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Open data practices are unevenly adopted across biomedical research; not all investigators share curated data for reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or reviewing, state your data sharing plan clearly and be realistic about norms in your subfield. Reviewers should recognize current heterogeneity; applicants should document how they will make data available and curated, if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex as a Biological Variable (SABV) must be considered in design
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs should consider male and female animals (SABV) where appropriate and report those variables; NIH policies have made this a review expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate SABV into experimental design, justify any single-sex studies, and describe analyses that will account for sex differences. Be aware this requirement can complicate design and review but is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of reviewer composition and potential conflicts when critiquing prior literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Study sections often include authors of the papers you cite or their academic 'homies', which can complicate how pointed critique of prior work is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame critiques of prior literature carefully and professionally; explain why limitations matter to your proposed work without gratuitous or ad hominem language. Where feasible, provide objective evidence (e.g., sample size, methodological flaws) rather than subjective judgments to reduce reviewer backlash.
